summary: Updates IMAP with persistent identifiers for mailboxes and messages, so clients can reuse cached data more efficiently when resources have moved on the server.

eli5.summary: Every folder and email gets a permanent ID tag, so even if it moves rooms, your phone still recognizes it.

questions: how do imap clients detect moved messages
subtitle: Gives IMAP mailboxes and messages permanent IDs, so a client can tell that something merely moved instead of downloading it again.

tldr.problem: When one IMAP client renames a mailbox or copies or moves messages, other clients connected to the same store cannot know the messages are identical, so they redownload everything.
tldr.mechanism: The OBJECTID extension adds a server-assigned MAILBOXID for mailboxes, an EMAILID for message content and an optional THREADID for related messages, with FETCH, STATUS and SEARCH support.
tldr.outcome: Clients can recognize renamed mailboxes and moved messages from their IDs and reuse cached data. The RFC updates RFC 3501 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8474 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3501 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Cache Problem
sections.content:
Many clients often use one IMAP store, and each may cache data so it does not have to download it again. RFC 3501 says a mailbox is identified by its name and UIDVALIDITY, and a message by that plus its UID. That triple is guaranteed to be immutable.

RFC 4315 adds a COPYUID response, so the client doing a copy can update its own cache. But any other client connected to the same store cannot know with certainty that the messages are identical, so it redownloads everything. The same holds for a rename done by another client.

This extension adds MAILBOXID and EMAILID properties so clients can quickly spot renamed mailboxes and moved messages. It also adds an optional THREADID. A server that does not implement threading returns NIL for every request for it. Servers advertise support by including OBJECTID in the CAPABILITY response.
sections.eli5: If a friend moves your toys to another shelf, you would have to count them all again. With a number sticker on each toy, you just check the stickers.

sections.title: What an ObjectID Looks Like
sections.content:
All ObjectID values are allocated by the server. An ObjectID is a string of 1 to 255 characters from a set of 64: a-z, A-Z, 0-9, the underscore and the hyphen. These are the same characters as base64url in RFC 4648, chosen because they are safe in filesystems, URIs and IMAP atoms. ObjectID values are case sensitive.

The RFC advises servers to avoid IDs that start with a dash or a digit, IDs that are only digits, IDs that differ only by ASCII case, and the three-character sequence NIL in any case, which could be mistaken for the IMAP null value. A good fix for most of these is to prefix every ID with a single letter.
sections.eli5: The sticker numbers use only letters, digits, dashes and underscores, so they never get mixed up with other things. Starting each one with a letter keeps it tidy.

sections.title: MAILBOXID for Mailboxes
sections.content:
The MAILBOXID is a server-allocated unique identifier for each mailbox. The server MUST return the same MAILBOXID for a mailbox with the same name and UIDVALIDITY, and MUST NOT report the same MAILBOXID for two mailboxes at the same time. When a mailbox is renamed in a way that keeps the same messages, the ID stays the same. Renaming INBOX is the exception, since RFC 3501 treats it as creating a new mailbox and moving the messages.

A client can get the ID in three places. A successful CREATE returns it as a MAILBOXID response code in the tagged OK. A successful SELECT or EXAMINE returns an untagged OK with the same code. And the STATUS command gains a MAILBOXID attribute; with the LIST-STATUS capability from RFC 5819 it can be combined with LIST.
sections.eli5: Each folder gets its own sticker when it is made. Renaming the folder does not change the sticker, so you can still tell it is the same folder.

sections.title: EMAILID and THREADID for Messages
sections.content:
EMAILID uniquely identifies the content of a single message. The server MUST return the same EMAILID for the same name, UIDVALIDITY and UID triple, and the same EMAILID as the source for the matching destination message after a COPY or MOVE (RFC 6851). It MAY give an APPENDed message an existing EMAILID if the content is exactly identical. The EMAILID identifies only immutable content, so messages with the same EMAILID can have different keywords, and the RFC does not define a way to STORE by EMAILID.

THREADID identifies a set of messages the server believes belong together. How it is calculated is left to the server; it is generally based on References, In-Reply-To and Subject, and RFC 5256 describes algorithms that could be used. The server MUST return the same THREADID for all messages with the same EMAILID, SHOULD return the same one for related messages even in different mailboxes, and MUST NOT change a THREADID once reported.

THREADID is optional. A server without it returns NIL in FETCH responses, and a SEARCH for THREADID must not match any messages. EMAILIDs and THREADIDs must never share a value; the RFC suggests prefixes such as M and T.
sections.eli5: Each letter gets a sticker for what is written in it, and a second sticker saying which conversation it belongs to. Letters in the same conversation share the second sticker.

sections.title: FETCH and SEARCH Support
sections.content:
Two new FETCH items, EMAILID and THREADID, return the matching response data items for each message. Two new SEARCH filters, EMAILID and THREADID, find messages whose ID is exactly the specified ObjectID.

The RFC's examples show the payoff. After a client moves message 2 to another mailbox, the message keeps its EMAILID when fetched from the destination, so a second client can recognize it. In the same example, two messages in one conversation share a THREADID while the third has its own.
sections.eli5: You can ask the server, "show me the stickers on all my letters," or "find the letter with this sticker."

sections.title: Advice for Clients and Servers
sections.content:
Clients that cache offline should fetch the EMAILID of all new messages to avoid redownloading details they already have. They should also fetch the MAILBOXID of any new mailboxes before discarding cache data for a mailbox that has vanished, so they can detect renames. Searching the all-mail mailbox with OR of EMAILIDs or THREADIDs is a fast way to find messages again after another client moved them.

Servers must be careful with proxies. MAILBOXID need only be unique within what is offered to one client login on one server hostname, but a proxy that aggregates several servers MUST NOT advertise OBJECTID unless it can guarantee that different objects never share an identifier.

If a client sees inconsistent ObjectIDs, for example identical IDs or IDs that changed when they must not, it SHOULD fall back to the guarantees of RFC 3501. It MAY instead discard its whole cache and resync, but it MUST ensure it cannot loop forever discarding and refetching the same data without user interaction.
sections.eli5: Check the stickers before you throw away your notes. If the stickers ever look wrong, go back to the old way of finding things, or start fresh, but never keep starting over forever.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Servers are strongly advised to generate ObjectIDs that are safe to use as filesystem names and unlikely to be autodetected as numbers. If a digest is used to generate IDs, it must be collision resistant, so implementers should follow current security research. Because the server makes the IDs, it can move to a new hash just by using it for new IDs, which is easy if each ID carries a prefix.

A digest-based ID may serve as proof that the server saw a particular sequence of bytes. That matters only if IDs leak to clients who are not allowed to fetch the data, so servers handling highly sensitive data should consider it. IANA added OBJECTID to the "IMAP Capabilities" registry and MAILBOXID to the "IMAP Response Codes" registry.
sections.eli5: A sticker number should not accidentally reveal secrets about what is inside the letter, so the server makes them carefully.

data.code:
C: 6 status foo (mailboxid)
S: * STATUS foo (MAILBOXID (F2212ea87-6097-4256-9d51-71338625))
S: 6 OK Completed
C: 8 rename foo renamed
S: * OK rename foo renamed
S: 8 OK Completed
C: 9 status renamed (mailboxid)
S: * STATUS renamed (MAILBOXID (F2212ea87-6097-4256-9d51-71338625))
S: 9 OK Completed

items.title: MAILBOXID
items.text: Identifies a mailbox and survives a rename.

items.title: EMAILID
items.text: Identifies the immutable content of one message.

items.title: THREADID
items.text: Optional; groups messages the server thinks are related.
